## Overview

A linear system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ can be read in two complementary ways.

- **Row picture**: each equation is a line (in 2D), a plane (in 3D), or a hyperplane
  (in $n$D). The solution is the point where all of them intersect.
- **Column picture**: the whole system is a single vector equation. The solution is the
  set of weights that combine the columns of $A$ into $\mathbf{b}$.

Both pictures describe the same solution. They also fail at the same time: when the
system is **singular**, the row picture loses its unique intersection point and the
column picture loses the ability to reach every $\mathbf{b}$. Understanding exactly how
they fail is the best way to understand why the good case works.

## Two Equations, Two Unknowns

Consider

$$
\begin{aligned}
2x - y &= 1 \\
x + y &= 5.
\end{aligned}
$$

### Row Picture

Each equation is a straight line in the $xy$-plane. The line $2x - y = 1$ passes through
$(\tfrac12, 0)$ and $(1, 1)$; the line $x + y = 5$ has slope $-1$. A point satisfies both
equations if and only if it lies on both lines, so the solution is their intersection,
$(x, y) = (2, 3)$.

### Column Picture

The same two equations are the two components of one vector equation:

$$
x \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
+ y \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now the unknowns are *weights*: how much of column 1 and how much of column 2 are
needed to produce $\mathbf{b}$. With $x = 2$ and $y = 3$,

$$
2 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + 3 \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}. \;✓
$$

Geometrically, $2(\text{column } 1)$ and $3(\text{column } 2)$ are two sides of a
parallelogram, and $\mathbf{b}$ is its diagonal. This is the parallelogram law of vector
addition, the same rule used for centuries to combine forces in mechanics.

::: {#cell-fig-2d-pictures .cell execution_count=1}

## Three Equations, Three Unknowns

$$
\begin{aligned}
2u + v + w &= 5 \\
4u - 6v \phantom{{}+w} &= -2 \\
-2u + 7v + 2w &= 9
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
$$

### Row Picture: Intersecting Planes

Each equation describes a plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

**Plane 1.** $2u + v + w = 5$ meets the axes at $(\tfrac52, 0, 0)$, $(0, 5, 0)$ and
$(0, 0, 5)$. A plane is fixed by any three of its points that are not collinear.

::: {.callout-note}
## The right-hand side only shifts the plane
The coefficients $(2, 1, 1)$ form the **normal vector** and fix the orientation of the
plane. Changing the right side moves the plane parallel to itself:
$2u + v + w = 10$ is the parallel plane twice as far from the origin, and
$2u + v + w = 0$ passes through the origin.
:::

**Plane 2.** $4u - 6v = -2$ has no $w$ term. That does not make it a line: $w$ is simply
free, so the plane is **vertical** (parallel to the $w$-axis). Even $u = 0$ is a plane
in 3D.

**Intersection.** Planes 1 and 2 meet in a line. Plane 3 cuts that line at a single
point, the solution

$$
(u, v, w) = (1, 1, 2).
$$

Check: $2 + 1 + 2 = 5$, $\;4 - 6 = -2$, $\;-2 + 7 + 4 = 9$. ✓

::: {#cell-fig-3d-row .cell execution_count=2}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Row picture in 3D: three planes meeting at the single point (1, 1, 2).](1_geometry_of_linear_eqns_files/figure-html/fig-3d-row-output-1.png){#fig-3d-row width=595 height=566}
:::
:::


### Column Picture: A Linear Combination

The same system as one vector equation:

$$
u \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}
+ v \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -6 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}
+ w \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{b}.
\tag{2}
$$

A vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$ can be viewed as a column of three numbers, as a point with
those coordinates, or as an arrow from the origin to that point. Whichever view is
used, only two operations matter:

- **Addition**, component by component:
  $(5,0,0) + (0,-2,0) + (0,0,9) = (5,-2,9)$.
- **Scalar multiplication**: $2\,(1,0,2) = (2,0,4)$, and $-2\,(1,0,2)$ points the
  opposite way.

Combining both operations gives a **linear combination**, the central idea of the
subject. The weights found in the row picture produce $\mathbf{b}$:

$$
1 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}
+ 1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -6 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}
+ 2 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

The numbers $(1, 1, 2)$ are simultaneously the **intersection point** in the row picture
and the **weights** in the column picture.

## Beyond Three Dimensions

With $n$ equations in $n$ unknowns:

| | Row picture | Column picture |
|---|---|---|
| Objects | $n$ hyperplanes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ | $n$ column vectors and $\mathbf{b}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ |
| Question | Where do all hyperplanes meet? | Which weights combine the columns into $\mathbf{b}$? |

A single equation $a_1 x_1 + \cdots + a_n x_n = b$ (with not all $a_i = 0$) defines a
**hyperplane**, a flat set of dimension $n - 1$. In the good case, each additional
equation cuts the dimension of the intersection by exactly one:

$$
n - 1 \;\to\; n - 2 \;\to\; \cdots \;\to\; 0.
$$

After all $n$ equations the intersection has dimension $0$: a single point, the solution.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Precise version
"Each equation lowers the dimension by one" holds exactly when the new equation's
coefficient row is not a combination of the previous rows. In general, if the system is
consistent, the solution set has dimension $n - r$, where $r$ is the number of
independent rows (the **rank**). The unique-solution case is $r = n$.
:::

## The Singular Case

### Row Picture: Four Ways to Fail

In 2D, the only way for two lines to fail is to be parallel. In 3D there are more
possibilities, and planes can fail without any two of them being parallel.

**(a) Two parallel planes.**
$2u + v + w = 5$ and $4u + 2v + 2w = 11$ have proportional normals $(2,1,1)$ and
$(4,2,2)$, but dividing the second by 2 gives $2u + v + w = 5.5$. Two distinct parallel
planes: no solution.

**(b) Three planes forming a "triangle."**

$$
\begin{aligned}
u + v + w &= 2 \\
2u \phantom{{}+v} + 3w &= 5 \\
3u + v + 4w &= 6
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
$$

No two planes are parallel, so every pair meets in a line. But the left side of
equation 3 is the sum of the first two left sides, while the right sides give
$2 + 5 = 7 \neq 6$. Thus

$$
(\text{eq. } 1) + (\text{eq. } 2) - (\text{eq. } 3): \quad 0 = 1,
$$

a contradiction. Seen end-on, the three lines of intersection are parallel and the
planes form a triangular prism: no common point.

**(c) A whole line of solutions.**
Change the last right side from $6$ to $7$. The same combination now gives $0 = 0$, so
equation 3 adds no new information. The third plane moves parallel to itself until it
contains the line where planes 1 and 2 meet. The system is still singular, but now it
has too many solutions rather than too few.

**(d) Three parallel planes.**
If all three normals are proportional, e.g.

$$
u + v + w = b_1, \qquad 2u + 2v + 2w = b_2, \qquad 3u + 3v + 3w = b_3,
$$

then for most $\mathbf{b}$ the three planes are distinct and parallel: no solution. For
special right sides with $b_1 = b_2/2 = b_3/3$ they coincide, and the whole plane is the
solution set. The right side $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}$ is always special: every equation
is satisfied by $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$, so every plane passes through the origin, and
parallel planes through a common point must be the same plane.

::: {.callout-note}
## Summary of the row picture
A singular system has either **no solution** (most right sides) or **infinitely many**
(special right sides). It never has exactly one.
:::

### Column Picture: Columns Trapped in a Plane

Write system (3) in column form:

$$
u \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}
+ v \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
+ w \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}
= \mathbf{b}.
\tag{4}
$$

Call the columns $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$. They lie in a common plane
through the origin, so every linear combination of them also lies in that plane.

- If $\mathbf{b}$ is **outside** the plane, no combination reaches it: no solution.
  This is the typical situation.
- If $\mathbf{b}$ is **inside** the plane, it can be reached in infinitely many ways.

**Why are the columns coplanar?** Find a nontrivial combination that gives zero:

$$
3\,\mathbf{a}_1 - \mathbf{a}_2 - 2\,\mathbf{a}_3
= \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix}
- \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
- \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 6 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}
= \mathbf{0}.
$$

So $3\mathbf{a}_1 = \mathbf{a}_2 + 2\mathbf{a}_3$: column 1 lies in the plane spanned by
columns 2 and 3, and only two of the three columns are independent.

**Which $\mathbf{b}$ lie in the plane?** A normal vector to the plane is

$$
\mathbf{a}_2 \times \mathbf{a}_3
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \times \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ -3 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}
\;\propto\; \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix},
$$

and indeed $\mathbf{a}_1 \cdot (1,1,-1) = 1 + 2 - 3 = 0$. Hence

$$
\mathbf{b} \text{ is reachable} \iff b_1 + b_2 - b_3 = 0.
$$

For $\mathbf{b} = (2,5,7)$: $2 + 5 - 7 = 0$, solvable. For $\mathbf{b} = (2,5,6)$:
$2 + 5 - 6 = 1 \neq 0$, not solvable.

::: {.callout-important}
## One vector, two roles
The vector $(1, 1, -1)$ is exactly the combination of **equations** used in the row
picture: $(\text{eq. } 1) + (\text{eq. } 2) - (\text{eq. } 3)$. The same vector that
combines the rows into $\mathbf{0}$ is perpendicular to every column. The solvability
condition $b_1 + b_2 - b_3 = 0$ is the right-hand side of that combination, which must
equal $0$ rather than $1$.
:::

::: {#cell-fig-3d-column-singular .cell execution_count=3}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Column picture of the singular system: all three columns lie in one plane. b = (2,5,7) lies in the plane (solvable); b = (2,5,6) does not.](1_geometry_of_linear_eqns_files/figure-html/fig-3d-column-singular-output-1.png){#fig-3d-column-singular width=663 height=614}
:::
:::


### The Complete Solution When $\mathbf{b}$ Is in the Plane

For $\mathbf{b} = (2,5,7)$, note that $\mathbf{a}_1 + \mathbf{a}_3 = (2,5,7)$, so
$(u,v,w) = (1, 0, 1)$ is one solution. Adding any multiple of $(3, -1, -2)$, which
produces $\mathbf{0}$, does not change the right side:

$$
\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ w \end{bmatrix}
= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{\text{particular solution}}
+ \; t \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}}_{A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}},
\qquad t \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

This is a line of solutions, matching configuration (c) in the row picture. The
structure "one particular solution plus every solution of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$"
holds for every consistent linear system.

## Rows Fail Exactly When Columns Fail

The column dependence above was not a coincidence. The rows were dependent
(row 1 + row 2 = row 3), and for a square matrix this forces the columns to be dependent
as well.

::: {.callout-important}
## Fact
For an $n \times n$ matrix $A$, the following are equivalent:

1. The $n$ hyperplanes do **not** meet in exactly one point (row picture breaks down).
2. The rows of $A$ are linearly dependent.
3. The columns of $A$ are linearly dependent, i.e. they lie in a common subspace of
   dimension less than $n$ (column picture breaks down).
:::

**Sketch of why rows dependent $\Rightarrow$ columns dependent.**

1. If some row is a combination of the others, elimination subtracts exactly that
   combination and produces a **zero row**.
2. A zero row means fewer than $n$ pivots, so at least one column has no pivot. Its
   unknown is a **free variable**.
3. Setting that free variable to $1$ and solving by back-substitution gives
   $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$ with $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$, which is precisely a
   nontrivial combination of the columns equal to $\mathbf{0}$.

The converse follows by applying the same argument to $A^{\mathsf T}$. This is a
structural fact rather than a numerical accident, and it holds in every dimension.

## Summary

| | Nonsingular | Singular |
|---|---|---|
| Row picture | $n$ hyperplanes meet in one point | No common point, or a line/plane/… of them |
| Column picture | Columns span all of $\mathbb{R}^n$; every $\mathbf{b}$ is reachable in one way | Columns lie in a lower-dimensional subspace; $\mathbf{b}$ reachable only if it lies there, then in infinitely many ways |
| Rows / columns | Independent | Dependent (both, always together) |
| Number of solutions | Exactly one | Zero or infinitely many |

The nonsingular case, where there is exactly one solution to be computed, is the
problem that elimination solves efficiently. The singular case, where one must describe
all solutions or decide that none exist, leads to the ideas of column space, null space,
and rank.
